Apollonian Circle

GeometryCirclesAlgebra
Game: This is a picture, not a game: it shows all the places that are the same number of times as far from A as from B.
How to play: Drag A, B, P or the dot beside A, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Slide the ratio bar, tick the boxes, and press Reset to start again.
1.536
Look for the math

Drag A or B and the orange circle moves, but P never leaves it: the number of times farther from A than from B stays the same all the way round.

The ratio makes a circle

Write the rule as AP / BP = r and square it. With P at (x, y), the terms in x² and y² cancel only when they have the same coefficient, and what is left is the equation of a circle of Apollonius. For A at a and B at b on a line, its centre is a + r²/(r²−1)·(b−a) and its radius is r·AB/|r²−1|. The logic test checks both formulas against the drawing for hundreds of positions.

Two points on the line AB

The applet builds the circle from two points on the line AB: D between A and B, and E outside it, with AD/BD = AE/BE = r. These are the feet of the internal and external bisectors — the angle bisector theorem in action. The circle with DE as its diameter is exactly the locus above: the test checks that D and E lie on it and that every sampled point on it has ratio r. Tick Hint to see the two lines from P to D and E.

What happens at r = 1

At r = 1 the formula divides by zero: there is no finite circle. The locus is the perpendicular bisector of AB — every point on it is equally far from A and B. The old applet faked this with a point a million pixels away; this page draws the exact line, as the verified cut-the-knot article states. The test samples forty points on that line and checks AP = BP at each one.

Inversion makes rings

Invert in the circle centred at A through the draggable dot R. Under this inversion, the locus circle becomes a circle centred at B′, the image of B, with radius R²/(r·AB). That is why all the circles for different r are nested and never cross: their images are rings around one centre. Tick Extra construction to see those rings and the images of P. The test confirms the radius formula and the nesting. One sentence on the old page says smaller r brings the circle nearer to B; the formulas show the opposite — small r hugs A and large r hugs B. The inventory's page address is the inversion proof, which does not embed the applet; the byline links to the verified article describing this same construction.

Set the slider to 1 and drag A and B: P always stays on the line that cuts AB in half at a right angle.
